title: Dunkelflaute: what it is, how to measure the risk, and how to fill the gap
label: 16 September 2026 · Dunkelflaute and electricity intermittency
summary: Experts from the Met Office, the Energy Systems Catapult and the University of Strathclyde explain that 'Dunkelflaute'—periods of low wind and low solar—is a useful shorthand but not a fixed technical measure. The real planning problem is the energy gap (residual demand) that can last days to weeks and needs long-duration storage, firm low-carbon generation or imported power. Climate change is unlikely to make these events dramatically more frequent, but demand patterns will shift. Models and transparency on assumptions (NESO and others) are needed, and solutions range from short-term batteries and thermal storage to large-scale molecular storage (hydrogen or gas in geological caverns) and possibly carbon capture; each option has cost, timing and policy constraints.

glossary.definition: A German term meaning a period of little wind and little sun, used to describe weather that reduces wind and solar generation.
The amount of electricity demand left to meet after subtracting generation from wind and solar.
Small-scale local generation, for example rooftop solar, that reduces the electricity seen by the transmission system.
National Energy System Operator — the UK body responsible for strategic energy planning and system resilience.
A unit of energy equal to one trillion watt-hours; used to measure large amounts of electricity storage or consumption.
A government-supported price guarantee to encourage investment in specific electricity generation technologies.
Technology that captures carbon dioxide from power or industrial plants and stores it underground to avoid emissions.
An electricity link between countries that lets them import or export power.

chapters.title: What Dunkelflaute is — and why it matters
chapters.takeaway: Dunkelflaute describes low wind and low sun, but planners focus on the resulting energy gap (residual demand) over hours, days or weeks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We're examining whether the Government understands how to fill the renewables gap when wind and sun are low—Dunkelflaute. Can you explain what it is from weather and energy perspectives?

turns.speaker: Professor Keith Bell
turns.text: In energy terms it's best seen as variability: when wind and solar output is low you get a 'residual demand'—the gap between demand and renewables. We quantify that over different periods—one day, a week, months—then model how to meet it.

turns.speaker: Dr Emily Wallace
turns.text: Meteorologically it's usually high pressure over northwest Europe: descending air brings dull skies and low winds. That can last days or weeks. If it's also cold, demand rises, so the system is hit on both supply and demand sides.

turns.speaker: Jon Saltmarsh
turns.text: Dunkelflaute is a useful shorthand. For planners we talk about 'gaps'—and especially about the timespan: a short flat day is manageable, but many slightly-below-average days can deplete storage over months.

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: Is it quantifiable? Can we set a baseline definition—some sources say 10 consecutive hours below 10% of capacity, for example.

turns.speaker: Dr Emily Wallace
turns.text: There's no single agreed definition. You can define it by wind and sunshine thresholds, residual demand, or by pressure patterns. Best practice is to look at cumulative impacts—duration and depth matter.

turns.speaker: Professor Keith Bell
turns.text: Exactly. You can model past weather over decades and report, say, the 95th percentile of the gap, but you still need a societal judgment on acceptable risk—it's never zero.

chapters.title: Predictability and climate change
chapters.takeaway: Short-term forecasting is improving; climate change is not expected to greatly increase Dunkelflaute frequency, but winters will generally warm and demand patterns will shift.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: How is the Met Office working with NESO and others to understand and predict Dunkelflaute risks?

turns.speaker: Dr Emily Wallace
turns.text: We have a formal partnership with NESO: daily forecasts, demand and generation inputs, and ensembles (thousands of simulations) for winter outlooks and longer-term stress tests. We also contributed to Royal Society work using simulated extremes beyond historical records.

turns.speaker: Lord Jay of Ewelme
turns.text: Will climate change make Dunkelflaute more common or longer?

turns.speaker: Dr Emily Wallace
turns.text: Wind and sunshine variability is large and models don't show a clear strong trend up or down; the climate signal is small relative to natural variability. Winters will warm on average, which tends to reduce heating demand, so Dunkelflaute frequency is not expected to rise clearly.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: Some say circulation patterns like the jet stream could change, causing new modes of weather—do you accept that?

turns.speaker: Dr Emily Wallace
turns.text: That's a complex modelling question. I offered to get a written response from the Met Office on the range of views; it's not something to answer off the cuff here.

turns.speaker: Professor Keith Bell
turns.text: Also remember correlations matter: if low wind days coincide with cold snaps, that's the worst-case. Even if climate trends are small, those compound events are critical to plan for.

chapters.title: Measuring the problem and who should provide transparency
chapters.takeaway: Quantify risk in terms of residual demand over relevant timescales, publish methods and assumptions, and NESO should lead with transparent modelling plus external critiques.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Parliament needs parameters to hold the system to account. What metrics should NESO use to assess Dunkelflaute risk?

turns.speaker: Professor Keith Bell
turns.text: Assess the residual demand (demand minus renewables) across multiple timescales and weather histories, using transparent models and long weather series. NESO should lead, but others should publish independent analyses to compare assumptions.

turns.speaker: Jon Saltmarsh
turns.text: Models make different compromises. The answer is not just a single definition of Dunkelflaute but transparent model inputs, assumptions and sensitivity tests so we can compare outcomes across approaches.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: Is there scope for faster, 'quick and dirty' public analyses to inform debate, rather than only slow peer-reviewed papers?

turns.speaker: Professor Keith Bell
turns.text: Yes — rapid analyses can help policy debate if they clearly state their limitations. NESO has been cautious and slow in places; more publicly available scenario detail would aid scrutiny.

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: You mentioned past episodes—what does history tell us?

turns.speaker: Jon Saltmarsh
turns.text: Royal Society work looked at 1980–2016 and found multi-day and even month-long low-output events in some years. In our 8-year look we found a two-week worst case creating roughly a 15 TWh gap under certain system mixes.

chapters.title: How to fill the gap: technologies, scale and costs
chapters.takeaway: Short-term balancing uses batteries and demand flexibility; long-duration needs molecular storage (hydrogen or gas in caverns) or firm low-carbon generation; each option faces cost, scale and policy barriers.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: Which technologies can handle hours vs days/weeks? What scales and timelines are realistic?

turns.speaker: Jon Saltmarsh
turns.text: Within-day: batteries and demand shifting; proven and scaling now. Long-duration (days to weeks): molecular storage—hydrogen or other gaseous fuels in geological caverns—or firm generation like nuclear or dispatchable biomass. Batteries are improving but today's battery capacity is gigawatt-hours, not terawatt-hours.

turns.speaker: Professor Keith Bell
turns.text: Cost trade-offs matter: batteries are high cost per terawatt-hour but efficient for short response; hydrogen and geological storage offer huge volumes at lower volume cost but need conversion plants and turbines, and investment to scale.

turns.speaker: Jon Saltmarsh
turns.text: To give numbers from the evidence: current grid batteries are around 18 GWh, pumped hydro about 12 GWh. Rough gas storage used to hold c.16–18 TWh. EVs could add up to ~2 TWh by mass adoption—still far below tens of TWh some scenarios suggest.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: What about thermal storage, tidal, wave, energy-from-waste—are these ignored?

turns.speaker: Jon Saltmarsh
turns.text: Thermal storage (heat batteries) is cheap and useful for short-to-medium durations. Marine energy has potential but today is costly; it needs cost reduction to compete. Energy-from-waste contributes but is small in scale and not zero carbon.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: Why has hydrogen storage stalled and how long would it take to deploy?

turns.speaker: Jon Saltmarsh
turns.text: Technically feasible, but big projects need large up-front capital (hundreds of millions to billions). Government funding and clear market mechanisms are needed to de-risk first-of-a-kind plants. Even then, multi-year lead times—roughly five to ten years to significant scale—are realistic.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: What about retaining gas plants beyond 2030 versus investing in CCS or hydrogen?

turns.speaker: Professor Keith Bell
turns.text: Some short-term reliance on unabated gas may be cheaper than building CCS for a rarely-used backup plant, but any unabated burn adds to the carbon budget. The choice depends on scale and frequency of use; it's a policy trade-off.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: Can interconnectors help when northern Europe is also affected?

turns.speaker: Jon Saltmarsh
turns.text: Interconnectors help most of the time because weather varies across Europe, but in broad high-pressure events much of northern Europe can be affected simultaneously, so interconnectors are not a guaranteed fix.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: Are market mechanisms adequate to get these technologies deployed?

turns.speaker: Jon Saltmarsh
turns.text: Contracts for difference helped drive wind. For rare, system-defining assets we may need different government interventions—direct investment, strategic purchasing or bespoke contracts—because private investors avoid first-of-a-kind risk.

turns.speaker: Professor Keith Bell
turns.text: There are new schemes—cap-and-floor, dispatchable power agreements—aimed at de-risking investments, but we need to monitor if they deliver at scale and speed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final point: you stressed modelling transparency and policy choices. What is the committee's clear request?

turns.speaker: Professor Keith Bell
turns.text: Ask NESO to publish clear, transparent scenario assumptions and residual-demand analyses; allow independent teams to compare models; and fund demonstration of long-duration storage and conversion chains so we can learn by doing.

turns.speaker: Dr Emily Wallace
turns.text: From the Met Office side: keep integrating rich weather datasets and extreme simulations into energy planning, and give NESO and industry the best forecasts and probabilistic guidance to inform risk-based decisions.

turns.speaker: Jon Saltmarsh
turns.text: And from Energy Systems Catapult: recognise this is a system-wide problem—coordinate short-term flexibility and long-term storage, set market signals to mobilise first-of-a-kind deployment, and be honest about the trade-offs.
